# SPHEREx Time-Domain Explorer: Making the Invisible Visible

SPHEREx Time-Domain Explorer is an AI-assisted citizen science platform that helps people explore how the universe changes over time using data from NASA's SPHEREx mission.

We developed a concept for an interactive web platform that retrieves astronomical observations and allows users to compare the same regions of the sky across different observation periods and infrared wavelengths. Features such as Blink Comparison, Difference Imaging, and Red-Cyan Overlay make moving objects and unusual changes easier to identify. An AI-assisted detection system analyzes image differences, estimates object movement, and highlights potential candidates, including asteroids, comets, and brown dwarfs. Users can then inspect, classify, and report interesting findings, contributing to a collaborative discovery process.

Our solution addresses the challenge of analyzing billions of astronomical observations by combining data visualization, automated analysis, and human participation. It makes complex space data more accessible, encourages public involvement in scientific research, and creates new opportunities to discover objects that might otherwise go unnoticed.

Project Details – SPHEREx Time-Domain Explorer

1. What does it do and how does it work?

SPHEREx Time-Domain Explorer is an AI-assisted astronomical exploration platform designed to help people discover changes in the universe through NASA's SPHEREx observations.

The platform collects astronomical image data from NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), including observations across 102 near-infrared spectral bands. It processes FITS images and aligns observations from different periods using World Coordinate System (WCS), allowing users to compare the same region of the sky accurately.

Users can explore the sky through an interactive viewer and investigate changes using three main visualization techniques:

  • Blink Comparator: Rapidly switches between observations to make moving objects easier to notice.
  • Difference Imaging: Highlights changes between two observations while reducing the appearance of relatively stationary sources.
  • Red-Cyan Overlay: Combines observations using different colors to reveal positional shifts.

An AI-assisted detection module analyzes image differences, estimates possible object movement, and identifies interesting candidates such as asteroids, comets, and brown dwarfs. Users can inspect these candidates, classify them, and submit reports through the citizen science system.

2. Benefits and Intended Impact

The main benefit is making complex astronomical data easier to explore and understand.

SPHEREx collects an enormous amount of information that is difficult for researchers to inspect manually. Our platform helps reduce this workload by combining automated candidate detection with human participation.

We aim to:

  • Help researchers identify potentially interesting moving objects more efficiently.
  • Make infrared astronomical observations accessible to people without advanced scientific knowledge.
  • Encourage students and astronomy enthusiasts to participate in scientific exploration.
  • Build a collaborative environment where users can contribute classifications and help prioritize unusual observations.

Our long-term goal is to connect AI technology, astronomical research, and public participation to support discoveries that might otherwise go unnoticed.

3. Tools, Programming Languages, and Technologies

Our selected technical architecture includes:

Frontend:

  • React and TypeScript for the web application.
  • Tailwind CSS for responsive interface design.
  • HTML5 Canvas and WebGL for astronomical image visualization.
  • Aladin Lite for interactive sky exploration.

Backend and Scientific Processing:

  • Python and FastAPI for backend services.
  • Astropy for astronomical data and coordinate processing.
  • NumPy and SciPy for numerical computation and image analysis.
  • Photutils for astronomical source detection.
  • OpenCV for image comparison and motion analysis.
  • Reproject for aligning astronomical images.

Data Sources:

  • NASA/IPAC IRSA and SPHEREx datasets.
  • Gaia Data Release 3 for supporting astrometric information.
  • WISE and WiseView as inspiration for time-based infrared image exploration.
  • NEOSSat and the Canadian Astronomy Data Centre (CADC) as additional astronomical resources.

The application is designed to work with publicly available mission data, without requiring specialized space hardware.

4. Creativity and Innovation

Our main creative idea is transforming astronomical image comparison into an interactive discovery experience.

Instead of simply displaying space images, we allow users to observe how the same region of the universe changes over time. Combining Blink Comparison, Difference Imaging, Red-Cyan Visualization, and AI-assisted detection creates an intuitive way to identify potential movement in astronomical observations.

We also introduce a Citizen Science approach that allows the public to participate in candidate classification and contribute to a shared discovery process.

5. Factors Considered During Development

Several important factors guide our design:

  • Scientific accuracy: Images must be aligned using astronomical coordinates, and potential detections must be distinguished from image artifacts and observational errors.
  • Data reliability: Results should retain observation timestamps, spectral information, and references to their original data sources.
  • Performance: Large FITS files and 102 spectral bands require efficient processing, optimized image delivery, and selective data loading.
  • Accessibility: The interface should be understandable and usable by people without an astronomy background.
  • Detection reliability: AI-generated candidates are preliminary findings that require further validation, not confirmed astronomical discoveries.
  • Scalability: The platform should support future datasets, additional observation periods, and a growing community of users.

Ultimately, SPHEREx Time-Domain Explorer aims to turn astronomical data into an accessible, collaborative discovery experience, helping more people explore the universe and contribute to scientific research.
